svg.data-layers: [{"k":"a","label":"The Still route","note":"Announced in 1874 and taught at Kirksville from 1892. The body contains what it needs for its own repair, repair depends on delivery, and delivery depends on unobstructed circulation. So a deranged structure starves the tissue. The rule of the artery is supreme."},{"k":"b","label":"The Palmer route","note":"1895. The same lesion in the same place, but the harm now travels by nerve rather than by blood. That is one hop apart in the mechanism and worlds apart in professional consequence."}]
svg.aria-label: Osteopathy and chiropractic put the lesion in the same place in the spine and then diverge on one hop: Still routes the harm through obstructed blood supply, Palmer through impinged nerve transmission.

g.data-tip: Both chains open on the identical claim: the trouble is a spinal segment out of position or not moving as it should. Both men treat it by hand and both refuse drugs. Nothing in the quarrel is about where the lesion sits.

Still located the harm in the circulation the tissues depend on for their own repair, and compressed the whole system into one line: the rule of the artery is supreme. Three years before 1895 he had already given it a school, a course of study and a diploma.

The end of the chain is the same word in both rows, and that is the point. Two incompatible mechanisms are being offered as the general account of illness, which is a great deal of weight for either one to carry.

Drawn twice because both routes start from it. Whether Palmer knew of Still's work the surviving record does not say, and historians generally find priority questions poorly formed anyway: the useful question is who built something durable around the idea.

Palmer's substitution, and the only one of the three senses of invention he can fairly claim. By 1910 The Chiropractor's Adjuster had stated it as a universal etiology: the great majority of disease results from vertebral displacement interfering with nerve transmission.

A specific claim is a falsifiable claim. Having proposed something this precise, chiropractic acquired an obligation to defend it precisely, and that obligation is what the twentieth century came to collect.

One hop, and the reason for it is not scientific. A distinct mechanism is a distinct territory: it gives a new group its own name for the lesion, its own account of why the neighbors are wrong, and its own claim to be doing something no one else can do.
